classification.difficultyReason: Requires recognising a perfect square in a parameterised Pythagorean calculation, handling both tangent signs and simplifying the resulting sums.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\sec\theta&=\frac{4a^2+1}{4a},\\\cos\theta&=\frac{4a}{4a^2+1}.\end{aligned}$$
Since $a>0$, $\cos\theta>0$, so $\theta$ is in quadrant I or IV, or on the positive $x$-axis.
For the reference triangle, take adjacent side $4a$ and hypotenuse $4a^2+1$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Opposite side}&=\sqrt{(4a^2+1)^2-(4a)^2}\\&=\sqrt{16a^4-8a^2+1}\\&=\sqrt{(4a^2-1)^2}\\&=|4a^2-1|.\end{aligned}$$
Thus the possible tangent values are
$$\begin{aligned}\tan\theta&=\pm\frac{|4a^2-1|}{4a}\\&=\pm\left(a-\frac{1}{4a}\right).\end{aligned}$$
The $\pm$ includes both signs, so the absolute value does not change this pair of possible values. When $a=\tfrac12$, the reference triangle degenerates and $\tan\theta=0$.
Hence
$$\begin{aligned}\sec\theta+\tan\theta&=a+\frac{1}{4a}+\left(a-\frac{1}{4a}\right)\\&=2a,\end{aligned}$$
or
$$\begin{aligned}\sec\theta+\tan\theta&=a+\frac{1}{4a}-\left(a-\frac{1}{4a}\right)\\&=\frac{1}{2a}.\end{aligned}$$
